newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss banks admit shame over Holocaust accounts.
newsitem.headline: Swiss banks admit shame over Holocaust accounts.

text.p: Swiss banks acknowledged "shame" that they had not done enough in 50 years to find the heirs of Holocaust victims and other owners of nearly 1,800 dormant accounts whose names were published worldwide on Wednesday.
Jewish leaders who have led an international battle for two years for the names of lost account holders praised the banks for breaking their strict code of secrecy.
But they made clear they only trusted the effort to find heirs because it would be supervised by an independent international commission headed by former U.S. central bank chairman Paul Volcker.

Swiss Bankers' Association chairman Georg Krayer said just a glance at the list published in newspapers in 27 countries and on the Internet (www.dormantaccounts.ch) showed names that clearly could have been tracked down by banks if they had tried.

The list provides over 1,870 names and their last known home towns from 1,785 accounts that today total 61.2 million Swiss francs ($41.2 million) -- 40 percent more than the banks last year acknowledged holding in dormant pre-1945 accounts.

"I was somewhat ashamed...I have not found a figleaf big enough to cover up the negligence of my banking colleagues in the period after the Second World War," Krayer told a joint news conference with Jewish leaders.
"With a little more effort we could have produced better results," he said.

The World Jewish Congress (WJC), which has led international protests over Swiss secrecy, said it was only satisfied now because claims to accounts already uncovered and others that may be found were being administered by an international body in which it has a part.
"We today have brought the Swiss banking system into the 20th century transparency mode," WJC secretary general Israel Singer said.

"When I speak about trust, I wasn't talking about the banks or this list or what hapened before today. I speak about a prospective trust that is based on these procedures that are taking place now," he added.

The list of foreign-held accounts opened before the end of World War Two is aimed at prompting potential heirs to make their claims to independent auditors overseen by a commission of Jewish, international and Swiss experts.

Swiss banks bowed to this process, which has been demanded by the WJC and allies for two years, after an earlier unilateral effort to satisfy bogged down claims which was rejected by powerful critics including the WJC and U.S. Senator Alphonse D'Amato.

In detail, the process starts with the published list in 19 languages that includes telephone numbers and addresses for requesting a claims information kit from auditors Atag & Young in five global offices -- New York, Tel Aviv, Basle, Budapest or Sydney.
The names of account-holders in the list ran from R. Joh. Aalberts in London to Dr. Karl G. Zwick in Cincinatti, followed by a shorter list of people holding proxy powers over dormant accounts.

Claims should be filed to the auditors within six months for a quick decision based on "relaxed rules of proof" adopted to soothe world anger after some banks demanded relatives show death certificates of family members murdered in Nazi camps.
No fees are charged for the claims and any disputes will be settled by a tribunal of experienced international arbitrators chaired by a Swiss but whose majority will not be Swiss.
The whole process should be complete in a year's time.
Volcker also heads an independent auditing commission set up by the banks and world Jewish groups last year to probe Swiss vaults and archives for traces of accounts left by Holocuast victims.

The list of names of foreigners will be followed in October by a second list detailing similar accounts opened by Swiss residents, who may have acted as proxies to hide away the assets of European Jews and others threatened by the Nazis.
